builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
summary: Sable replaces trusted, unverifiable inference with a cryptographic argument that a committed integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence bit for bit, using a 31-bit prime constraint system, Reed-Solomon/BLAKE3/BaseFold commitments, and a single-GPU streaming prover. It costs 41-50x serving latency per proved request, requires redefining the model as a deterministic integer function F_O whose greedy output matches BF16 only 86.3% of positions (within 1.6-1.7 points on MMLU/GSM8K), and the proof is not zero-knowledge, so it applies only to open-weight models. It can fail operationally when bit-exact equivalence to the deployed floating-point model is required, since F_O diverges from BF16 outputs at a nontrivial rate and verified results certify the quantized surrogate rather than the original model.
rationale: The prover fits constrained hardware and the per-request cost is low, but verifiable-inference proofs are only worth adopting when the deployment has an actual audit or trust requirement, which most small-team serving workloads lack.
technique: Single-GPU ZK proof of bit-exact LLM inference

claims.statement: Sable replaces trusted, unverifiable inference with a cryptographic argument that a committed integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence bit for bit, using a 31-bit prime constraint system, Reed-Solomon/BLAKE3/BaseFold commitments, and a single-GPU streaming prover. It costs 41-50x serving latency per proved request, requires redefining the model as a deterministic integer function F_O whose greedy output matches BF16 only 86.3% of positions (within 1.6-1.7 points on MMLU/GSM8K), and the proof is not zero-knowledge, so it applies only to open-weight models. It can fail operationally when bit-exact equivalence to the deployed floating-point model is required, since F_O diverges from BF16 outputs at a nontrivial rate and verified results certify the quantized surrogate rather than the original model.

Proves 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens (398 s for 16,384 tokens) on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell; 41 to 50 times serving time, about 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM.
